I have run construction sites for eighteen years, and most of the expensive mistakes I have seen started with a bad instruction. Not a wrong one, a vague one. A good instruction on site has four parts. Who does it, what exactly, by when, and how you will check it. People usually remember the first two and forget the last two. But an instruction with no deadline is not an instruction. It is a suggestion, and on site a suggestion is done when somebody has time. So I give every instruction with a time, and then I ask the person to repeat it back to me. Some new foremen think that is a little insulting. It is not. It costs ten seconds, and a misunderstanding on a construction site can cost you a week.

The best boss I ever had was a construction director in Texas. Every Monday at seven, he walked the site with the foremen, and he gave each of us three priorities for the week. Only three. He never did our work for us, even when it was faster for him to do it himself, and believe me, sometimes it was. If something went wrong, he wanted to hear about it from us before he heard it from anybody else, so we kept him posted all the time. And he finished every instruction with the same question: what do you need from me to get this done? Twenty years later, I am a foreman with my own crew, and I still ask that question every Monday.
